## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāpadumajātaka* (Ja 472) belongs to the Twelfth Nipāta (*Dvādasakanipāta*) of the Jātaka collection [Burlingame 1921]. According to its commentary, the Buddha told this story while residing at Jetavana concerning Ciñcā Māṇavikā, who had falsely accused him of sexual misconduct and subsequently met with ruin [SuttaCentral; Braarvig; Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1887]. The core narrative illustrates the widespread folklore motif of "Potiphar's wife" [Silk 2009; Aris & Aung San Suu Kyi 1979]. When King Brahmadatta departs to suppress a border uprising, he leaves Prince Paduma (the Bodhisatta) in charge of the realm [Anandajoti 2010; Silk 2009; Aris & Aung San Suu Kyi 1979]. Upon the king's return, Paduma's stepmother is enamored by the prince and attempts to seduce him, but he staunchly rejects her advances [Braarvig; Anandajoti 2010; Silk 2009; Aris & Aung San Suu Kyi 1979]. Rejected, she scratches herself to simulate assault and accuses the prince of rape [Silk 2009; Aris & Aung San Suu Kyi 1979]. The king rashly orders his son thrown down a precipice, but Paduma is saved through his loving-kindness (*mettā*) by a mountain deity, given refuge by a nāga king, and ultimately renounces the world [Fausböll 1887]. The central moral verses emphasize righteous kingship, specifically warning that a king must never inflict punishment without thoroughly and personally investigating all the facts [Burlingame 1921; Anandajoti 2010]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), Ciñcā Māṇavikā is identified as the stepmother, Devadatta as the father, Ānanda as the nāga, Sāriputta as the mountain deity, and the Bodhisatta as Prince Paduma [Fausböll 1887].

Text-reuse computations by DharmaNexus align substantial segments of the canonical verses with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (11 matches in the fourth volume and 8 matches in the sixth volume) [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pāli, DharmaNexus detects cross-language matches with the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada* (7 matches) and the Chinese *Qishi yinben jing* (起世因本經, T 25, 2 matches) [DharmaNexus]. In secondary studies, the narrative background is compared with other treatments of Ciñcā's slander such as the *Pusa chu tai jing* and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [Burlingame 1921; Legittimo 2006], and scenes from the jātaka are identified in Buddhist art at Amaravati [Francis 2002].
